For people who design and deliver programs

Remove a hurdle.
Check whether it worked.

Six concrete starting points for a WIC agency and its partners. Pick the step where families are getting stuck, assign an owner, and test the change.

01 / Outreach lead

Make referrals lead to an appointment.

Give each partner a single referral route with clinic contact details, the next step, and a consent-based callback option. Assign a staff member to unresolved referrals.

Start here

This week: test the referral from a prenatal clinic and a pediatric office. Record every handoff and unanswered call.

Measure it & check the boundaries

Measure

For each referral cohort, count contacted ÷ referred and enrolled ÷ referred within a defined period. Separate pending cases from people who decline.

Pilot a 30-day follow-up window; do not treat it as an official WIC deadline.

02 / Clinic operations

Send the document checklist before the visit.

Name the accepted proofs of identity, residence, and income. Explain alternatives and whom to call if a document is missing. Provide translated and accessible versions.

Start here

This week: compare the appointment reminder with what staff actually request. Remove conflicting or duplicative instructions.

Measure it & check the boundaries

Measure

Track appointments completed on the first attempt and repeat document requests. Review by language and appointment channel where privacy permits.

Confirm accepted documents and verification rules with the state agency; change the instructions, not eligibility policy.

03 / Scheduling lead

Offer a workable way to finish enrollment.

Ask about preferred contact times. Show available appointment formats clearly. Offer permitted remote options, and keep a staffed phone route for people who cannot complete a digital process.

Start here

This week: review a sample of missed appointments. Call with consent to learn whether timing, travel, technology, or another issue mattered.

Measure it & check the boundaries

Measure

Compare time from first contact to completed certification, no-shows, and completed reschedules. Track staff workload alongside participant completion.

Remote procedures depend on current agency authority. Do not promise remote certification where it is unavailable.

04 / Retail liaison

Fix the failed checkout, not just the leaflet.

Create a way to report a rejected item with store, date, product code, and error message. Check shelf labels against the approved-product list. Give shoppers a clear escalation contact.

Start here

This week: walk through one real shopping trip with a consenting participant, compensate their time, and resolve the problems found with the retailer.

Measure it & check the boundaries

Measure

Count resolved ÷ reported checkout problems and median time to resolution. Redemption alone does not identify the reason for an unused benefit.

Avoid collecting names or full receipts when an item code and store are enough.

05 / Retention lead

Make renewal a next step people can see.

Before the current visit ends, explain when renewal is due, what can be reused, and how to reschedule. Send reminders in the person’s chosen channel; provide an easy reply or callback route.

Start here

This week: test one reminder with families. Ask them to show what they would do next; revise any instruction they cannot act on.

Measure it & check the boundaries

Measure

Track renewal completion and gaps in issuance among people whose continuing eligibility is established. Record age-outs, moves, voluntary departures, and unknown reasons separately.

A missed renewal is not proof of continuing eligibility or lack of need.

06 / Evaluation lead

Measure where people stop—and whether a change helps.

Track referral, contact, appointment, certification, first redemption, and renewal as separate events. Choose one bottleneck and pilot one change with a comparable group or staged rollout.

Start here

This week: define each event, its denominator, and the follow-up window before changing the process. Publish a short baseline and review date.

Measure it & check the boundaries

Measure

Report completion rates, time, participant burden, and staff workload. Show uncertainty and missing data. Ask people who stop what happened.

These are proposed tests, not guaranteed effect sizes. A before/after change alone cannot establish causation.

A first-month plan.

  1. Week 1: choose one hurdle, name the owner, and record the baseline.
  2. Week 2: test the revised step with participants and frontline staff; fix what they cannot complete.
  3. Week 3: run a small pilot with a comparison where feasible.
  4. Week 4: review early completion and burden measures. Continue following longer-term outcomes before declaring success.
Evidence behind these recommendations

These are editorial recommendations informed by documented barriers and implementation work. They are not six interventions with proven effect sizes.

  • New Hampshire/Vermont interviews, 2024: referrals, eligibility awareness, staff contact, and competing demands.
  • USDA participant survey, 2019: awareness, scheduling, retention, and changing perceived need; samples differ.
  • Massachusetts caregiver interviews, 2020–2021: product fit, labeling, shopping tools, and positive staff support.
  • USDA modernization evaluation, 2024 annual report: implementation context for outreach and service changes; early implementation is not proof of impact.

Adapt to current state policy, participant consent, language access, and disability access. Measure reach without treating every nonparticipant as someone who wants to enroll.
